Implementation Plan

## Plan: Overwrite smoke canary file

Planning ref: `a1c3d7d16f5a166c395e84a79dff9b0a5106af60` (branch `main`). The integration branch mismatch line reads `unknown`, not `true`, so the plan goes ahead.

## Files likely to change
- `tests/e2e_smoke_canary.txt`

## Acceptance
ACCEPTANCE: check CI
ACCEPTANCE: post-merge none: this is a data-only canary file with no deploy or post-merge workflow

## Functions or modules to implement
None. Replace the whole content of `tests/e2e_smoke_canary.txt` with exactly these bytes:
`status: ok\nrun_id: 43115910623\nupdated-by: ai-pipeline\n`

That is three lines, each ending in LF, with no trailing blank line, no header and no BOM.

## Data structures affected
None.

## API or interface changes
None.

## Decisions
### D1 — Overwrite the whole file instead of editing it line by line
- Chosen: write the file in full with the exact three lines (the equivalent of the `printf` command in the issue).
- Alternatives considered: editing the existing lines one at a time.
- Why: the issue asks for a complete replacement. Writing the full file guarantees no old lines are left behind.

## Security considerations
- No trust boundary, endpoint, secret or money surface is touched.
- The content is fixed text taken from the issue. It is not run or interpreted anywhere.

## Potential risks or edge cases
- A missing trailing newline, or an extra blank line, would break the exact-content check. Confirm afterwards with `od -c` or `wc -l`, which should report 3 lines.
- No other file may change. `git diff --stat` should list only this file.

## Testing considerations
- Check the result with `printf 'status: ok\nrun_id: 43115910623\nupdated-by: ai-pipeline\n' | cmp - tests/e2e_smoke_canary.txt`. It should exit 0.
- No new tests are needed.

Scope-mode: Hold Scope
Reuse-audit: extends tests/e2e_smoke_canary.txt
Scope-mode justification: The issue fully specifies a single-file content replacement with explicit constraints to touch nothing else. Holding scope to that one file meets every requirement; there is no shortcut-versus-complete trade-off, so the §6 priority order (Security > Correctness & safety > Backward compatibility > Operational clarity > Performance > Speed) is satisfied by an exact, verified overwrite.
